meaning.text: Its names point to its connection with the heavenly flame and with fire in general: zhar means the glowing coals in a stove, and zhary the hot season of summer.
Its name is enough to show its close connection with flame or light.

appearance.text: Its feathers blaze with a silvery or golden sheen.
In one tale its feather shines like fire.

scene.text: It dwells in a golden cage.
In the depth of the night it flies into a garden and lights it up as brightly as a thousand burning fires.
In one tale it flies every night into a king's garden to steal the golden fruit of an apple tree.
In a Russian tale the golden apples it steals ripen during the night.
In one tale, at dawn in a forest, the forest begins to roar and the sea rises in waves as it flies up, lights on the ground and pecks at scattered wheat.

appearance.text: The Ptak Ohnivak's feathers are red-gold.

behavior_habitat.text: According to Bohemian legends, its song heals the sick and restores sight to the blind.
The Czechs are convinced that its singing heals illnesses and takes blindness from the eyes.
According to a Croatian version, it feeds on magic grasses instead of golden apples.
In the Carinthian tradition, instead of golden apples it steals ripe grapes from a famous vine that gave a bucket of wine every hour.
In the Carinthian tradition, its gall restores lost sight.
In a version from the Bukovina, while the hero lies dead after his brothers carry the bird off, the bird is silent and its cage is lustreless.
In the same version, when the hero comes back to life the bird starts its magic song again and its cage flashes anew like fire.
A single feather from its tail lights up a dark room.
A tale says such a feather is worth more than a whole kingdom, and the bird itself is beyond price.
It feeds on golden apples which have the power of bestowing youth and beauty.
The golden apples it feeds on give eternal youth, beauty and immortality.
When it sings, pearls pour from its open beak.
It sinks into a death-like slumber when the day dawns and wakes to fresh life after sunset.
In one tale it sleeps soundly all day, and at night its owner flies about on it.
In the same tale it carries a princess far away on its back at night.
In the same tale it plunges a prince into a magic slumber.
In the same tale, when the day begins to dawn during a flight, the bird sinks lower and lower and falls to the ground.
In the same tale its wings, cut off and worn by the princess, rustle around her and hold back a prince who eats a man every night.
In one tale it brings a murdered prince back to life by gathering his scattered pieces, putting them together and sprinkling them with dead water and then live water carried in its beak.

dealing_with_it.text: In one tale the youngest prince, keeping watch in the garden at night, fails to capture it but secures one of its tail-feathers.
In the same tale the hero takes the bird out of its golden cage, but trying to carry off the cage as well sounds an alarm and he is taken prisoner.
In another tale a hunter scatters wheat on the ground and hides behind a tree at dawn; when the bird pecks the wheat his steed sets a hoof on its wing so that it can be bound with cords.
In a variant of that tale it is caught with a trap: a cage strewn with pearls large and small.

rationale.text: The verified rows name six peoples: Russians and Czechs and Slovaks (Afanasyev), Slovenes (Afanasyev's Carinthian tradition), Croatians and Czechs (Ralston), and Ukrainians (Ralston's Bukovina version).
Afanasyev (1865) describes the bird for Rus' and records the Czech-Slovak name and red-gold feathers, the Carinthian grapes and gall, and the Czech belief in its healing song.

Ralston's general description, the Croatian version and the Bohemian legends on p.285 cite no source, and the tale on p.284 is footnoted to Khudyakov, not Afanasyev; on those passages Ralston counts as independent, though the p.285 description runs close to Afanasyev's 1865 wording.
Ralston's skazka retellings on pp.235, 286 and 287 are footnoted to "Afanasief, vii." and are counted with Afanasyev, not as an independent source.
Both authors independently record the Czech healing-song belief (Ralston's "Bohemian legends", Afanasyev's "Чехи убѣждены"), so more than one people rests on more than one independent author.

notes.text: origin: no page says where the firebird comes from or who becomes one. Searched firebird, fire bird, fire-bird, zhar, жар-птица, жаръ-птиц, жар-птиц in all sources. Afanasyev's mythological reading (afanasyev1865:p.513, the bird as an embodiment of the thunder god like Agni; afanasyev1868:p.295, the image mixing the sun and lightning) and Ralston's comparison with the Phoenix (ralston1873:p.286) are scholarly interpretations, not folk accounts of origin, and were left out.

related: no page opened links the firebird to another pilot creature. afanasyev1869:p.159 says that in the Carinthian redaction of the golden-apple tale nine vilas take the place of the firebird; that page was read only at the hit and is a substitution in one tale, not a stated relation, so no related row was written.

Variant name Ptak Ohnivak: Afanasyev's Latin-script form is OCR-garbled ("р і а к ОЬпіѵак") and Ralston's footnote prints "Ptak Ohnivdk"; no clean native form could be copied as printed, so the variant has no native row. Afanasyev prints the Cyrillic genitive "птака Огнивака" only.

Ralston's footnotes were not used for lore: p.285 glosses zhar-ptitsa as "the glow-bird" and p.284 says "Ornithologically, the Zhar-ptitsa is the Cassowary"; afanasyev1865:p.514 footnote 3 says the bird carries wandering heroes on its wings in some tales. Ralston's main text says the chap-book tale on p.286 is "of doubtful origin".

Most behaviour and capture clauses come from single Russian skazkas retold by Ralston (one a chap-book story he calls of doubtful origin) and are hedged as "in one tale". afanasyev1868:p.386 (Slavic tales: the hero plucks a tail feather that shines at night like the sun) was opened but not used beyond confirming the feather motif.
appearance_forms: no conflicting descriptions; the Czech-Slovak red-gold feathers are kept in their own variant.
Editorial: the firebird of Stravinsky's ballet The Firebird (1910) and of later stage, film and game adaptations is excluded; this entry records only the cited folk sources.
